title: Paid family & medical leave
position: Strong support for establishing a state paid family and medical leave insurance program.
core_argument: No working family should have to choose between a paycheck and caring for ʻohana. 90% public approval. California's 20+ year program shows mothers retain higher incomes and reduce SNAP reliance.
standard_ask: Pass the bill as drafted; preserve the social-insurance model with shared employee+employer contributions.

title: Pay transparency & wage equity
position: Strong support for closing the small-employer carve-out in pay transparency law.
core_argument: Hawaiʻi women earn 82.4–87% of men, *backsliding* from 92.8% in 2014. With equal pay, overall poverty drops 5.4%→2.5%; single-mother poverty 21.3%→10.7%.
standard_ask: Apply pay transparency to all employers; transparency is the precondition for accountability.

title: Health coverage continuity
position: Strong support for state bridge coverage as federal Medicaid is cut.
core_argument: Federal Medicaid cuts cause "churn" — eligible people lose coverage to paperwork, not ineligibility. State must bridge for undocumented, seasonal, and independent workers. UH survey: 19% of residents carry medical debt ≥$500; 20% delay care.
standard_ask: Establish bridge coverage; tie eligibility to circumstance, not status.

title: Capital gains tax equalization
position: Support raising the capital gains rate; ultimate goal is equalization with ordinary income (11%).
core_argument: Hawaiʻi taxes capital gains at 7.25% vs. ordinary income at 11% — a loophole that benefits the wealthy. 70% of Hawaiʻi capital gains are earned by filers with >$400k income; the rate primarily affects those above $783k. Generates ~$55M.
standard_ask: Raise to at least 9% this session; equalize with ordinary income next.

title: REIT income tax
position: Support actually taxing REITs — not another study.
core_argument: Hawaiʻi exempts REIT income despite REITs holding $17B+ in Hawaiʻi assets. In 2014 REITs reported $900M in Hawaiʻi income and paid $0 in state corporate income tax.
standard_ask: Strike the study language and impose the tax this session.

title: Millionaire's income surcharge
position: Strong support for a 2% surcharge on income above $1M.
core_argument: Generates ~$71M annually (Medicaid funding). Top 1% pays an additional ~0.72% of income. Massachusetts adopted a similar surcharge and saw continued wealth growth post-tax — the "wealth flight" argument is empirically wrong.
standard_ask: Pass without watering down the threshold or the rate.

title: Freeze and adjust Act 46
position: Strong support for freezing Act 46 (2024 income tax cuts) and adjusting top brackets up.
core_argument: Act 46 cuts are unevenly distributed and cost the state billions. Freezing the rollout and adjusting the top 5 brackets up by 0.25–1 percentage points generates ~$69M, 86% of which comes from the top 1%.
standard_ask: Freeze and adjust; treat this as a measured fiscal correction, not an attack.

title: Medical debt forgiveness
position: Strong support for state-funded medical debt acquisition and forgiveness.
core_argument: Use the proven non-profit acquisition model (27 states/cities now do this) to forgive medical debt for households ≤400% FPL or with debt ≥5% of income. Medical debt cascades into delayed care, housing instability, and worse health.
standard_ask: Fund the program at the level needed to retire material debt for eligible households.

title: Conveyance tax modernization
position: Strong support for marginal-rate conveyance tax with progressive rate structure and dedicated revenue.
core_argument: The conveyance tax hasn't been updated since 2009. Modernize to marginal rates; protect <$2.2M owner-occupied homes; raise rates on high-value investment properties; index to inflation. Dedicate revenue: affordable housing (20%), DHHL (30%), DURF (20%), conservation (5%). Hawaiʻi needs 50,000+ housing units; DHHL waitlist is 6,000 families ($800M backlog).
standard_ask: Pass HB2049 as drafted; resist amendments that strip the dedicated funding allocations.

title: Renter protections
core_argument: 38% of Hawaiʻi households rent. Maui and Kauaʻi have among the highest median rents in the country. Renters are routinely sidelined in housing policy despite carrying the highest cost burden.

title: Housing tax credits
position: Support strengthening WCTC, federal/state EITC, and a state-level child tax credit.
core_argument: 15,664 residents left Hawaiʻi in 2022 due to cost of living. Refundable tax credits put money in working families' hands for everyday expenses — food, rent, medical care.

title: Universal free school meals
position: Strong support for universal free school meals.
core_argument: "School meals are essential school supplies." 3 in 10 households with children face food insecurity. The current means-tested system fails: a family of 4 earning $47k+ doesn't qualify, even though ~$107k is needed to cover living costs in Hawaiʻi. 34% of denied students are actually eligible — they fall through the paperwork. For some keiki, school meals are the only balanced meals they receive.
standard_ask: Pass HB1779; pass HB2296; reject phase-ins that delay implementation past 2030.

title: SNAP access
position: Strong support for extending SNAP certification and adopting the federal ESAP waiver.
core_argument: 160,000+ Hawaiʻi residents depend on SNAP. Extending certification from 12→24 months and adopting ESAP (up to 36 months for seniors) reduces "churn" — eligible people losing benefits to paperwork. 23 states already use ESAP.
standard_ask: Pass without rollback; align with federal options.

title: Transit equity
position: Support fare-free transit for keiki, state employees, and pursuit of universal fare-free.
core_argument: Removing cost barriers expands youth and disability access. Locally proven: Maui <24 fare-free, Hawaiʻi County fully fare-free. Nationally proven: Washington state free <18, Kansas City fare-free saw ridership surge.

title: Pedestrian safety
position: Strong support for Leading Pedestrian Intervals (LPIs) and Accessible Pedestrian Signals (APS).
core_argument: A 3–7 second head start at intersections measurably saves lives. Seattle: 48% reduction in turning collisions, 34% reduction in serious/fatal pedestrian injuries. NYC 2025 results: 33% injury reduction, 65% fatal reduction. Installation cost: hundreds to a few thousand dollars per intersection. Disproportionately benefits keiki, kūpuna, people with disabilities, and those relying on walking and transit.
standard_ask: Pass with funding for HDOT to deploy at high-risk intersections statewide.

title: Over-broad tax cuts
position: Oppose sweeping, untargeted tax cuts that drain the general fund without helping working families.
core_argument: HB2404's over-broad cuts created major budget trouble; the benefit skews to higher earners while the revenue loss threatens services low- and moderate-income families rely on.

position: Oppose estate-tax break bills (trickle-down giveaways to the wealthiest estates).
core_argument: Estate-tax breaks are bad policy for Hawaiʻi — they concentrate wealth and cost revenue with no broad benefit.
